claims.feature: other: what Kay actually did on the Silmarillion

claims.feature: other: biography of the Silmarillion year

verdicts.trueWording: he created the final publish work with Guy Kay's help
verdicts.note: Live page (200). Kane's answer to the 'what made you decide a book should be written' question contains the quote verbatim, in the sentence saying Christopher Tolkien 'provided just as remarkably little insight into the final step of the process'. Every limb (Kane speaking; remarkably little insight; final step; Kay's help) supported.

verdicts.trueWording: Kane's answer seems to be yes
verdicts.note: Live page (200). Ordway's review closes a paragraph with a rhetorical question asking whether the cumulative effect of the edits sufficed to change Tolkien's prose style for the worse, then the quoted sentence. Page says 'these edits' where the claim says 'editorial cuts'; the referenced edits explicitly include removal of descriptive detail, so the limb holds.

verdicts.trueWording: he became an editor of The Silmarillion in 1974 (Ordway 140)
verdicts.note: Live page (200). BrightWeavings header states it is the 2012 honours thesis by Matthew Rettino written at McGill; the quoted clause with its parenthetical Ordway citation stands in the opening abstract/introduction paragraph before section 'I. Theory of Fantasy and Historical Fiction'.

verdicts.trueWording: The strongest single literary influence on Kay's creation of The Fionavar
verdicts.note: Live page (200). In section 'I. The Fionavar Tapestry' the sentence continues by naming Tolkien and calling it a natural enough result after Kay co-edited The Silmarillion with Christopher Tolkien; both limbs supported.

verdicts.trueWording: Coles writes that Kay has an ease with crafting words
verdicts.unsupportedLimb: 'the poet Don Coles' - the page never describes Coles as a poet (it calls Kay a poet); Coles is introduced only as writer of the introduction
verdicts.note: Live page (200). Third body paragraph reads 'In his introduction to the collection, Don Coles quotes a line of Kay's verse ... Whether in prose or poetry,' then the quoted clause verbatim. Introduction, collection and the prose-or-poetry limb all check out; only the 'poet' epithet is absent from the page.

verdicts.trueWording: nods towards his relationship with J. R. R. Tolkien
verdicts.note: Live page (200). Sentence names the poem 'If I Should Fly Across the Sea Again' and adds 'to whom the poem is dedicated', supporting the dedication limb. Paragraph is the last body paragraph, not the sixth as the claim's page field says; that is a locator, not a limb.

verdicts.trueWording: every detail is seamlessly woven into her astonishing tapestries
verdicts.note: Live host returned 403 to both browser UAs; reached via Wayback raw capture https://web.archive.org/web/20240616085027id_/... In the section bylined 'Marie Macpherson, author of The Knox Trilogy', the sentence continues ': the profusion of sounds, tastes, colours, and textures offer a sensory experience', and is preceded by 'Painstakingly researched'. All limbs supported.

verdicts.trueWording: author and keynote speaker @ DD Centenary Gathering 2023
verdicts.note: Same Wayback capture (live host 403). The string is the byline under the 'Guy Gavriel Kay' heading, verbatim including the '@'.

verdicts.trueWording: she was wonderful in person, not just in print
verdicts.note: Same Wayback capture (live host 403). Kay's contribution reads that from the first meeting 'and through many other encounters' the quoted clause follows, supporting the many-encounters limb.

verdicts.trueWording: working on the papers that became The Silmarillion
verdicts.note: Live page (200), BrightWeavings reproduction headed 'This appreciation first appeared in Locus Magazine, December 2001.' First paragraph: Kay met Dunnett in the spring of 1975 while living in a village called Hanney just outside Oxford, then the quoted clause. All four limbs (1975, spring, village outside Oxford, Silmarillion papers) supported.

verdicts.trueWording: which was a part of the editing process
verdicts.note: Live page (200). First paragraph: going through the Tolkien correspondence is followed by the quoted parenthesis verbatim; Kay is the one doing it, so the 'he worked on' limb holds.

verdicts.trueWording: I didn't discuss the details of editing The Silmarillion
verdicts.note: Live page (200). Parenthesis continues 'then, and still don't', inside the paragraph describing the three-hour conversation at Dunnett's house following the spring 1975 call, so both the 1975/Dunnett limb and the still-does-not limb hold. It is the third body paragraph, not the fourth.

verdicts.trueWording: enticed me into a paper chase as I tried to locate
verdicts.note: Live page (200) at digitalmedievalist.com, titled 'The Books of Dorothy Dunnett - Celtic Studies Resources', copyright line names Lisa L. Spangenberg. Opening paragraph credits the enormous quantity of literary allusions and quotations in the Lymond Chronicles, then the quoted clause, ending 'Dunnett's sources.'

verdicts.trueWording: offer the sources and even the translations, for many of the allusions
verdicts.note: Same live page, section 'The Dorothy Dunnet Companions'; subject of the sentence is 'The two Companions books', and the page lists The Dorothy Dunnett Companion and Companion II. Claim's 'supply' paraphrases the page's 'offer'; quote itself is verbatim.

verdicts.trueWording: had to look up the former
verdicts.note: Live page (200), post dated August 5, 2026, byline 'bill', on Bill's Dunnett Blog. Paragraph glosses epithalamium then elegy and asks 'I wonder what percentage of readers had to look up the former to make sure they understood it?!' - 'the former' is epithalamium, as the claim reads.
